ex_en: This man is our new neighbour.
note: pl. رجالة rjāla / رجال rjāl. راجلي rājli = my husband.

ex_en: This woman works at the hospital.
note: pl. نسوان niswān / نسا nsa. With a possessive it becomes مرت- mart-: مرتي marti = my wife.

ex_en: This child has been crying since the morning.
note: pl. أطفال aTfāl. Libyans also say صغار Sghār for 'kids'.

ex_en: The kids are playing in the house.
note: pl. صغار Sghār. Also an adjective 'small'; as a noun الصغار = the children.

ex_en: The baby is asleep, lower your voice.
note: From European 'bebè/baby'; very common in Libyan homes. Formal: رضيع raDī3.

ex_en: I have one son and two daughters.
note: pl. أولاد awlād / ولاد wlād. ولدي wildi = my son. زوز zōz = two (Libyan).

ex_ar: البنت هذي تقرا معاي في الجامعة.
ex_tr: il-bint hādhi tigra m3āy fi l-jām3a.
ex_en: This girl studies with me at university.
Whose little boy is this?
This little girl is lovely, God protect her.
note: Diminutive of بنت bint; pl. بنيّات bnayyāt.

ex_en: My friend is coming from Benghazi today.
note: pl. صحاب S7āb. Also means 'owner' (صاحب الحوش = owner of the house).

ex_en: I went with my (female) friend to the market.
This is my friend from school days.
note: pl. رفاق rfāg / رفقة. ق pronounced g.

ex_en: Our neighbour is a very kind man.
The neighbour brought us a plate of bazeen.
note: pl. جارات jārāt. بازين bāzīn = Libyan national dish.

ex_en: We have guests tonight.
note: pl. ضيوف Dyūf. Hospitality to ضيوف is a point of honour in Libya.

ex_en: There's a person waiting for you outside.
note: pl. أشخاص ashkhāS. In speech واحد wā7id 'someone' is also very common.

ex_en: People in Tripoli love the sea.
The guys went to play football.
note: Used as a friendly address: يا شباب yā shbāb = hey guys.

ex_en: This young man works at the bank.
This young woman is a new doctor.

ex_ar: الشيباني هذا يعرف تاريخ المدينة كله.
ex_tr: ish-shībāni hādha ya3rif tārīkh il-mdīna kullah.
ex_en: This old man knows the whole history of the city.
note: pl. شيابين shyābīn. Libyan/Maghrebi word, from شيب 'grey hair'.

ex_en: This old woman tells lovely folk tales.
note: pl. عجايز 3jāyiz. خرّافة kharrāfa = folk tale.

ex_ar: السلام عليكم يا حاج، كيف حالك؟
ex_en: Peace be upon you, sir, how are you?
note: Respectful address for any older man, pilgrimage or not. Fem. حاجة 7ājja.

ex_en: The old lady cooked soup for us.
note: Respectful address for an older woman.

ex_en: The tribal elder solved the problem.
The grown-ups are sitting in the guest room.
note: pl. of كبير kbīr. مربوعة marbū3a = Libyan sitting room for guests.

ex_en: The whole group came to the wedding.

ex_tr: ma tiftaHsh il-bāb li ayy gharīb.
ex_en: Don't open the door to any stranger.

ex_ar: فيه أجانب ياسر يخدموا في الشركة.
ex_tr: fīh ajānib yāsir yikhdmu fi sh-sharika.
ex_en: Many foreigners work at the company.
I'm a Libyan from Misrata.
note: pl. ليبيين lībiyyīn; fem. ليبية lībiyya.

ex_en: This charity helps orphans.
I don't have an enemy in the world.
May God keep your children for you.
note: Libyan/Bedouin word for one's kids; very common in blessings.

ex_ar: جدي كان بدوي يعيش في الخيمة.
ex_tr: jiddi kān badwi y3īsh fi l-khēma.
ex_en: My grandfather was a Bedouin who lived in a tent.
Today's generation loves the phone a lot.
My mother cooks the best couscous.
note: pl. أمهات ummahāt. Also الوالدة il-wālda (polite).

ex_en: My father works in Tripoli.
note: Libyan form: بوي būy = my father, بوك būk = your father. Also used in names/nicknames (بو بكر). pl. آباء ābā'.

ex_en: Dad brought us sweets.
note: Affectionate, used by children and adults.

ex_en: Mum, where's the key?
My late father was a teacher.
note: الوالدين il-wāldēn = parents. Fem. والدة wālda.

ex_en: My older brother lives in Misrata.
note: Libyan: خوي khūy = my brother. pl. خوت khūt (خوتي khūti = my brothers/siblings).

ex_en: My sister studies medicine.
My (paternal) uncle is coming to have lunch with us.
note: pl. عمام 3mām. A wife may also call her father-in-law عمي 3ammi.

ex_en: My paternal aunt lives near us.
My maternal uncle has a house in the countryside.
My maternal aunt brought a present for the baby.
My grandfather is ninety years old.
My grandmother tells us folk tales.
note: pl. جدات jiddāt. See also حنّا 7anna.

ex_en: Granny made us asida.
note: Libyan affectionate word for grandmother (حنّي 7anni = my granny). عصيدة 3aSīda = traditional porridge.

ex_en: My cousin (paternal uncle's son) lives in Benghazi.
note: pl. ولاد عم wlād 3amm. Also used loosely for close kin/tribe.

ex_ar: بنت عمي تعرّست الصيف اللي فات.
ex_en: My cousin got married last summer.
My cousin (maternal uncle's son) works with me.

ex_ar: بنت خالي تقرا في كلية الهندسة.
ex_tr: bint khāli tigra fi kulliyyit il-handasa.
ex_en: My cousin studies in the engineering faculty.
My cousin (maternal aunt's son) is coming to visit us.
note: Arabic distinguishes cousins by which parent's sibling they come from.

ex_en: Her husband works abroad.
note: Formal-ish; in daily speech راجلها rājilha 'her man' is more common. Careful: زوز zōz = 'two'.

ex_en: His wife is a dentist.
note: Daily speech prefers مرته martah 'his woman' or حرمته 7urmtah.

ex_en: Give my regards to your wife and kids.
note: Polite, indirect way to refer to someone's wife.

ex_en: My family is big, I have seven siblings.

ex_ar: نبي نمشي نزور أهلي في العيد.
ex_tr: nibbi nimshi nzūr ahli fi l-3īd.
ex_en: I want to go visit my family for Eid.
All the relatives came to the funeral gathering.
note: sg. قريب grīb. ق pronounced g.

ex_ar: كل واحد في ليبيا يعرف قبيلته.
ex_tr: kull wā7id fi lībya ya3rif gbīltah.
ex_en: Everyone in Libya knows their tribe.
note: pl. قبايل gbāyil. Tribal ties remain important in Libyan social life.

ex_en: My in-law is a respectable man.
note: pl. نسابة nsāba. Covers male in-laws broadly.

ex_en: My mother-in-law loves me a lot.
note: Also called خالتي khālti or عمتي 3ammti out of politeness.

ex_en: The bride is wearing a traditional wrap and Libyan jewellery.
note: pl. عرايس 3rāyis. Also used for a doll and for a sandwich (عروسة تن).

ex_en: The groom came in the decorated car.
Her fiancé works as an engineer.
I brought a present for my fiancée.
The old man has twenty grandchildren.
I named my first granddaughter after my mother.

ex_ar: الأرملة هذي تربي في أربع صغار.
ex_tr: il-armla hādhi trabbi fi arba3 Sghār.
ex_en: This widow is raising four kids.
note: pl. أرامل arāmil. Masc. أرمل armal.

ex_en: These kids are twins.
note: Also heard as توام twām in Maghrebi speech.

ex_en: How many siblings do you have?
note: pl. of خو khū. Libyan form.

ex_en: My head has been hurting since morning.
Her eyes are blue.
Wash your hands before eating.
My foot hurts from walking.
note: dual رجلين rijlēn. Also كراع kurā3 for 'leg' in Maghrebi speech.

ex_en: He's kind-hearted.
note: pl. قلوب glūb. ق pronounced g.

ex_en: Her hair is long and black.
note: Collective; one hair = شعرة sha3ra. أكحل ak7al = black (Libyan).

ex_en: Close your mouth while you eat.
I have a tooth that hurts.
My wisdom tooth came through.
My nose is blocked from the cold.
note: pl. خشوم khshūm. Libyan word; MSA أنف is not used in daily speech.

ex_en: My ear hurts.
note: dual وذنين widhnēn; pl. وذان wdhān.

ex_en: Wash your face and come.
He has a sharp tongue (lit. long tongue).
My lips are chapped from the cold.
She kissed her on the cheek.
Put your hand on his forehead, he's hot.
Her eyebrows are thin.
His eyelashes are long.
My father has a white beard.
He grew a moustache like his grandfather.
note: sg. شارب shārib; the plural is used for one moustache.

ex_en: My neck hurts from the pillow.
My throat is burning.
I carried the bag on my shoulder.
He broke his arm in the match.
I hit my elbow on the door.
I cut my finger with the knife.
Cut your nails.
My back hurts from work.
He has a pain in his chest.
My stomach hurts, I ate too much.
note: pl. كروش krūsh. The everyday Libyan word for tummy.

ex_en: He has a stomach problem.
He slept on his stomach.
The baby's navel stump hasn't fallen off yet.
I fell and grazed my knee.
He has a torn thigh muscle.

ex_ar: كعبي يوجع فيا من الصباط الجديد.
ex_tr: ka3bi yūja3 fiyya min iS-SabbāT il-jdīd.
ex_en: My heel hurts from the new shoes.
note: pl. كعوب k3ūb. Also 'heel of a shoe'.

ex_en: You need to look after your body.
My skin is dry in winter.
Blood came out of his nose.
A bone in his leg broke.
Use your brain!
He has a liver disease.
note: Also used affectionately: يا كبدتي yā kibdti 'my darling'.

ex_en: He had a kidney operation.
Smoking harms the lungs.
He has an intestinal inflammation.
I saw tears in his eyes.
He has a bruise on his shin.
She read his palm.
note: pl. كفوف kfūf. Also 'slap': عطاه كف = he slapped him.

ex_en: You need to go to the doctor today.
note: pl. دكاترة dakātra. Fem. دكتورة doktōra. The everyday word; طبيب Tbīb is more formal.

ex_en: The physician told me to rest for a week.
note: pl. أطباء aTibbā'. جمعة jum3a = week (Libyan).

ex_en: Take the medicine after eating.
Is there a pharmacy open tonight?
They took him to the hospital by ambulance.
note: From Italian ospedale (via Maghrebi). pl. سبيطارات sbīTārāt. مستشفى mustashfa is also used.

ex_en: Tripoli Central Hospital is big.
note: pl. مستشفيات mustashfayāt. Used in official names.

ex_en: The clinic opens at nine.
note: pl. عيادات 3yādāt. Private clinics are very common in Libya.

ex_en: The little one has had a fever since yesterday.
note: Libyan/Maghrebi, from سخون skhūn 'hot'. MSA حمّى 7umma.

ex_en: I caught a cold from the chilly weather.
note: Also خذاني البرد khdhāni l-bard 'the cold got me'.

ex_en: Be careful you don't catch a cold.
He has a cough that won't go away.
I have a pain in my back.
note: pl. أوجاع awjā3. Verb يوجع yūja3: راسي يوجع فيا = my head hurts.

ex_en: I have a headache from the noise.
He has a migraine.
This wound needs stitches.
The injury to his knee is minor.
He has a fracture in his arm.
They put a cast on him for a month.
This illness is contagious.
The patient is waiting for the doctor.

ex_ar: خوذ حبة الصبح وحبة في الليل.
ex_en: Take one pill in the morning and one at night.
The little one is afraid of injections.
The doctor ordered a blood test.
The nurse gave me the injection.
Call the ambulance quickly!
My father had heart surgery.
My grandfather has diabetes.
note: In speech diabetes is simply السكر 'the sugar'.

ex_ar: خالي عنده الضغط، ما ياكلش ملح.
ex_en: My uncle has high blood pressure, he doesn't eat salt.
I have a dust allergy.
He went abroad for treatment; the treatment is expensive.
note: Many Libyans travel to Tunisia for علاج.

ex_en: Health is the most important thing.
note: صحة! Sa77a = 'bless you / enjoy' (said after eating or a haircut).

ex_en: Take his temperature, he looks hot.
I got dizzy while standing.

ex_ar: الصغير عنده إسهال، اعطيه ما ياسر.
ex_en: The little one has diarrhoea, give him lots of water.
I have an itch on my hand.
She burned her hand in the kitchen.

ex_ar: فيه ورم في رجله من الضربة.
ex_tr: fīh waram fi rijlah min iD-Darba.
ex_en: There's swelling on his foot from the knock.
I have an appointment with the dentist.
Kids need vaccinations before school.
I feel very tired today.
note: Also 'effort': تعبك ما يضيعش = your effort won't be wasted.

ex_en: His wife is in the hospital to give birth.
The pharmacist asked for the prescription.
Wrap the wound with gauze.
My eyesight has got weaker, I need glasses.
Put on your clothes, we're going out.
note: Lit. 'things'; Libyan everyday word for clothes. sg. حاجة 7āja 'thing'.

ex_en: This outfit suits you.
I bought a white shirt for the wedding.
note: pl. قمايج gmāyij. Maghrebi form of قميص.

ex_en: These trousers are too long for me.
note: pl. سراويل srāwīl. بنطلون banTalōn is also used.

ex_en: Take off your shoes before you come in.
note: pl. صبابيط Sbābīṭ. Maghrebi word (cf. Spanish zapato / Italian ciabatta).

ex_en: Wear your slippers in the house.
Take the jacket, the weather's cold.
note: From Italian giacchetta / French jaquette. pl. جاكيتات.

ex_en: I wore the black coat in winter.
note: From Italian cappotto. pl. كبابيط kbābīT.

ex_en: She bought a new dress for Eid.
This skirt is very short.
My sister wears the hijab.
She wore a black abaya.

ex_ar: جدتي كانت تلبس الفراشية كي تطلع.
ex_tr: jiddti kānat tilbis il-farrāshiyya kay tiTla3.
ex_en: My grandmother used to wear the farrashiya when she went out.
note: Traditional Libyan white woollen or silk wrap covering the whole body; now worn mainly by older women or at weddings.

ex_ar: العريس لابس الجرد في ليلة الحنة.
ex_tr: il-3rīs lābis il-jard fi lēlt il-7inna.
ex_en: The groom is wearing the jard on henna night.
note: Large woollen wrap draped over the shoulder; a symbol of Libyan traditional dress. pl. جرود jrūd.

ex_en: This hawli is hand-woven.
note: Libyan traditional wrap, often worn by women; similar to the jard.

ex_en: He wore the farmla over the shirt.
note: Traditional Libyan embroidered vest, part of formal men's dress. pl. فرامل frāmil.

ex_en: My father wears the kabbous on Friday.
note: Red (or black) felt cap worn with traditional dress; also called شنّة shanna.

ex_en: The red shanna is part of our ancestors' dress.
note: Synonym of كبوس kabbūs, typical of Libyan men's traditional dress. pl. شنن.

ex_en: He put on the white skullcap for prayer.
note: pl. طواقي Twāgi. ق pronounced g.

ex_en: He wore a white jubba on Eid day.

ex_tr: libs badla u krāfaTTa li l-mgābla.
ex_en: He wore a suit and tie for the interview.
note: pl. بدل bidal. بدلة عربية = traditional Libyan outfit.

ex_en: I don't like wearing a tie.
Wear a light T-shirt, it's hot.
note: Maghrebi word (from Italian maglia/Spanish). pl. مراويل mrāwīl.

ex_en: The kids are wearing shorts at the beach.
I like wearing jeans and a shirt.
I put on my pyjamas and went to sleep.
My socks are torn.
I put the phone in the bag.
This handbag is very expensive.
I forgot my wallet at home.
Where did I put my glasses?
note: Also نظارة naDHDHāra. نظارات شمس = sunglasses.

ex_en: The trousers are loose, I need a belt.
note: pl. حزامات / أحزمة. Also seat belt.

ex_en: She wrapped the scarf around her neck.
Give me a tissue to wipe my nose.
This ring is made of gold.
I bought her earrings for Eid.
note: pl. حلقان. Also خرص khurS in Maghrebi speech.

ex_en: She's wearing a gold chain.
The money's in my pocket.
The bride is wearing a traditional Libyan necklace.
Come, let's have lunch at home.
note: pl. حيشان 7ēshān. In Libya حوش = the whole house (originally a courtyard house), while بيت = a room.

ex_en: The house has four rooms.
note: pl. بيوت byūt. Libyan: بيت = room (MSA 'house'). بيت النوم = bedroom.

ex_en: The old house is in the old city.
note: pl. ديار dyār. Less common than حوش in Tripoli speech.

ex_ar: ساكنين في شقة في الدور التالت.
ex_tr: sāknīn fi shigga fi d-dōr it-tālit.
ex_en: We live in an apartment on the third floor.
note: pl. شقق shigag. ق pronounced g.

ex_en: My mother is in the kitchen cooking.
The bathroom is at the end of the hallway.
Where's the toilet, please?
note: From French/Italian. Also بيت الما bēt il-ma.

ex_en: Show the guests into the sitting room.
note: Distinctly Libyan: a (usually square) reception room near the entrance where men receive guests. pl. مرابيع mrābī3.

ex_en: We're watching TV in the living room.
The bedroom has a big window.
Close the door behind you.
Open the window, it's hot.
note: pl. شبابيك shbābīk. حلّ 7all = to open (Libyan).

ex_en: The light is coming in through the small window.
note: pl. طاقات Tāgāt / طيقان. Traditional houses have small طاقات.

ex_en: The ceiling is leaking from the rain.
note: pl. سقوف sgūf. ق pronounced g.

ex_en: I hung the clothes out on the roof.
note: pl. سطوح sTū7. Flat roofs are used for drying laundry.

ex_en: Go up the stairs slowly.
note: sg. درجة daraja (one step). Also درج daraj.

ex_en: I left the key inside the house.
Hang the picture on the wall.
The floor is wet, watch out.
I live on the second floor.
note: pl. أدوار adwār. Also 'turn': دورك dōrak = your turn.

ex_en: We drink tea on the balcony.
Put the car in the garage.
We bought new furniture for the house.
note: Collective noun. أثاث athāth is the formal word.

ex_en: This bed is very comfortable.
This mattress is hard.
note: pl. مطارح mTāri7. Also floor mattresses for seating guests.

ex_en: Give me another pillow.
It's a cold night, bring a blanket.
Put the plates on the table.
note: From Italian tavola. pl. طاولات Tāwlāt.

ex_en: Sit on the chair.
He fell asleep on the sofa in the living room.
The clothes are in the wardrobe.
The books are on the shelf.
He looked at himself in the mirror.
Close the curtain, the sun is strong.
The cold water is in the fridge.
Turn on the TV, there's a match.
Put the clothes in the washing machine.
The AC is broken and it's hot.
note: pl. مكيفات. A wall unit is often called سبليت splīt.

ex_en: Turn on the heater, it's very cold.
A fan isn't enough in summer.
Put the cake in the oven.
The power has been out since morning.
note: Libyan: الضو = the electricity supply as well as light. pl. أضواء aDwā'.

ex_en: The bulb has burnt out, change it.
The charger is in the socket.
This carpet is handmade.

ex_ar: الكليم هذا جابته جدتي من الجبل.
ex_tr: il-klīm hādha jābitah jiddti min ij-jbal.
ex_en: My grandmother brought this kilim from the mountains.
note: pl. كلايم klāyim. Traditional Libyan woven rug.

ex_en: We removed the carpet and put down marble.
The tap drips all night.
I want to take a shower.
Give me a towel to dry off with.
Wash your hands with soap.
Bring the broom, let's clean the house.
Fill the bucket with water.
Take the rubbish out.
The iron is hot, be careful.
The tank on the roof is empty.
note: pl. خزانات. Many Libyan homes store water in roof tanks.

ex_en: Someone rang the doorbell.
The iron gate needs painting.
Light a candle, the power's out.
Put the teapot on the fire.
note: pl. برارد brārid / برادات. Central to Libyan tea (شاهي) culture.

ex_en: Give me a glass of water.
I washed the dishes after lunch.
The big pot is for feasts.
Careful, the knife is sharp.
Apartment rent is expensive in Tripoli.
The whole house floor is marble.
